lead: A contour is a line on the ground whose every point has the same reduced level (RL, height above datum). Draw many contours and the ground's shape lies flat on paper: the spacing between lines reads as slope. Surveyors use contours to choose a site, align a road or canal, plan drainage, site a reservoir, and estimate cut and fill. This chapter defines the contour interval and horizontal equivalent, reads contour patterns, and compares direct and indirect methods.
prereq: You need Chapter 3.1 for reduced level; map scale and topographic sheets come from Unit 1.

blocks.text: A contour joins points of equal RL. The contour interval (CI, also called the vertical interval in some syllabi) is the fixed RL step between neighbouring contours, for example 2 m. The horizontal equivalent (HE) is the ground distance between two such contours at a place; it is not fixed for the whole map.

On a slope of angle θ, HE = CI ÷ tan θ. A steep slope has a small HE, so its contours sit close together. A flat slope has a large HE, so its contours spread out. On a 1:1000 map, a ground HE of 20 m appears as 20 m ÷ 1000 = 0.020 m = 20 mm.

blocks.where: HE is horizontal equivalent in metres; CI is contour interval in metres; θ is ground slope in degrees.

blocks.text: Choose CI from four things: purpose (a dam site needs finer detail than a regional map), scale (a small-scale sheet cannot carry fine contours), ground slope (steep ground closes up), and time and cost (every smaller step means more field readings).

items: A contour closes on itself, inside the sheet or beyond its edge. If it runs off the sheet, the loop is completed outside.
Contours of different RL never cross. They may meet only at a vertical cliff or overhang, where the ground is not a single-valued surface; such a feature is drawn with a cliff symbol.
Close contours mean steep ground; wide contours mean flat ground. Spacing alone does not give height.
Evenly spaced contours mean a uniform slope. Straight parallel contours mean a plane slope.
Across a valley, the contour bends upstream, towards higher ground; the V points uphill. Across a ridge, it bends downstream, towards lower ground; the V points downhill.
Water flows down the steepest path, at right angles to contours, from high RL to low RL.
A contour is not drawn through a building, bridge or vertical cut; the map uses a symbol for the structure.

blocks.text: The spacing rule follows from HE = CI ÷ tan θ: doubling the slope halves the spacing. Read a contoured map by following each bend and asking whether it points to higher or lower ground.

In direct contouring, the surveyor fixes points that lie on one chosen contour. Set up the level, take a backsight on a benchmark, and compute the height of instrument (HI). For a contour of RL Hc, the required staff reading is HI − Hc. Move the staff until the reading matches; peg that point. Repeat along the contour, then tape between pegs. Do this for each contour. Direct work is accurate and simple on open, flat ground, but slow on steep or bushy land.
In indirect contouring, spot levels are measured first and contours are interpolated later. Four field layouts are common:

items: Cross-sections: level along a centre line and at offsets, for a road, canal or rail line.
Grid squares: peg a grid, say 10 m to 30 m, and take the RL at every grid point.
Tacheometry: a tacheometer gives horizontal distance and RL of many points from one setup.
Radial lines: run rays from a central station and take levels along each ray.

blocks.text: Interpolation assumes the ground slopes uniformly between two adjacent spot levels. For a contour RL H<sub>c</sub> between points A and B:

blocks.where: x is distance from A in metres; H<sub>A</sub> and H<sub>B</sub> are the reduced levels of A and B in metres; H<sub>c</sub> is the contour level in metres; L is the horizontal distance AB in metres.

blocks.text: If H<sub>c</sub> lies outside the range H<sub>A</sub> to H<sub>B</sub>, that contour does not cross AB.

A factory or airstrip needs flat land and gentle access; contours show where to avoid deep cut. A road follows a grade, and a canal often follows a contour or a fixed gradient, so alignment is chosen to balance cut and fill. Contours show catchment divides and flow paths for drainage; water crosses contours at right angles. A dam is placed across a valley where a contour closes upstream, and the stored water is bounded by the contour at full supply level. Comparing existing and proposed contours shows depth of cut or fill. A straight line drawn on the map gives a profile from the spot levels where it crosses contours. Volume from those areas is in Chapter 3.7.

examples.question: Two adjacent grid points A and B are 30 m apart. Their reduced levels are 102.6 m and 105.1 m. The contour interval is 2 m. Locate the 104 m contour on the line AB and state whether the 106 m contour crosses AB.
steps: Contours at a 2 m interval between these heights: 104 m. The 106 m contour is above B, so it does not cross AB.
Rise from A to the 104 m contour = 104.0 − 102.6 = 1.4 m.
examples.answer: The 104 m contour lies 16.8 m from the point of RL 102.6 m, and the 106 m contour does not cross AB.

traps: The V of a contour in a valley points upstream, towards higher ground. Water flows downstream, but the contour bends the other way.
One contour interval does not fit every map. A 1:1000 site plan may use 0.25 to 0.5 m; a 1:50,000 topographic sheet uses 10 or 20 m.
Close contours mean steep ground, not high ground. A flat plateau at 2000 m can have widely spaced contours.
Contour interval is a vertical RL step; horizontal equivalent is a ground distance. Do not multiply CI by scale to get HE; divide CI by tan θ.
Contours of different RL never cross except at a cliff or overhang. A crossing on a normal map is a drawing error.

quiz.a: The vertical distance or RL step between two consecutive contours, for example 2 m.

quiz.q: Why does a contour bend upstream when it crosses a valley?
quiz.a: The contour must stay at one RL. As the valley sides rise upstream, the same RL is reached farther upstream, so the line bends towards higher ground and its V points uphill.

quiz.q: Two points A and B are 40 m apart with RL 50.2 m and 53.2 m. The contour interval is 1 m. Find where the 52 m contour crosses AB, measured from A.
quiz.a: RL difference = 3.0 m. Rise to 52 m = 52.0 − 50.2 = 1.8 m. Fraction = 1.8 ÷ 3.0 = 0.6. Distance from A = 0.6 × 40 m = 24 m.

quiz.q: On a 1:5000 map the spacing between two contours is 4 mm. The contour interval is 5 m. Find the ground slope as a percentage.
quiz.a: Ground spacing = 4 mm × 5000 = 20000 mm = 20 m. Slope = CI ÷ ground spacing = 5 ÷ 20 = 0.25 = 25%.

quiz.q: A map shows evenly spaced, straight, parallel contours. What does this say about the ground, and what use does it have?
quiz.a: It is a uniform plane slope: equal rise over equal horizontal distance. Such ground suits a straight road or canal grade, and cut and fill can be estimated from a section.

quiz.q: Why is a contour map needed before siting a reservoir dam?
quiz.a: The map shows the valley shape, the catchment divide, and the area flooded at the full supply level. A narrow gorge with a closing contour upstream gives a short dam and a large storage volume.

quiz.q: Distinguish direct and indirect contouring in one sentence each.
quiz.a: Direct contouring pegs points on each chosen contour in the field; indirect contouring measures spot levels and interpolates the contours between them.
The ground distance between two consecutive contours at a place; it equals CI ÷ tan θ.

beyond: Not for the exam. In practice, contours come from a digital elevation model (DEM) built from total station, GNSS, LiDAR or drone photogrammetry, and GIS software draws them at any interval. Civil engineers use the same surface for earthwork volumes, flood levels and drainage design. Search for DEM, TIN, LiDAR ground filtering, and contour generation in QGIS.
